dashboard.label: Start here
dashboard.description: What this app does, what its numbers mean, and what they do not.

div.h2: Riskability finds known vulnerabilities in the software your fleet actually has installed — using CVE databases you carry in by hand.
div.p: It is built for search heads that can never reach the internet. Nothing here calls out to anything: the vulnerability data arrives as a file you build on a connected machine and import on the Feed administration page, and the inventory arrives from swinv through your forwarders.

The most important thing to know about every number in this app: an empty panel means nothing was found, which is not the same as there is nothing to find. A feed that was never imported, a host that stopped reporting, and a package no advisory covers all produce the same reassuring zero. That is why the three clocks below come first, and why Coverage exists at all.

search.query: | inputlookup riskability_feedstate_lookup | search _key=current | eval days = round((now() - imported_at) / 86400, 1) | fields days

single.option: days since the CVE data was imported

search.query: | inputlookup riskability_hoststate_lookup | stats max(host_last_scan) AS t | eval hours = round((now() - t) / 3600, 1) | fields hours

single.option: hours since any host last reported

search.query: | inputlookup riskability_matchstate_lookup | stats max(matched_at) AS t | eval hours = round((now() - t) / 3600, 1) | fields hours

single.option: hours since inventory was compared to the feed

search.query: | inputlookup riskability_hoststate_lookup | stats count AS n

html.div: Every number in this app is only as current as the oldest of those three. A fresh scan compared against a six-month-old feed finds six-month-old vulnerabilities.

single.option: excluded on purpose, with a recorded reason

search.query: | inputlookup riskability_matchstate_lookup | stats sum(n_components) AS n

div.p: Not just the package manager. It looks inside container images, snap bases and chroots, and records the path of every copy it finds — which is how this app can tell a patched host from one with a stale copy still sitting in an image.

A PURL when a package manager installed it (pkg:deb/ubuntu/openssl), or a CPE when nothing did — which is most Windows software. A PURL is read from a package record; a CPE is inferred from a display name. That difference is why Windows findings are always reported at low confidence.

div.b: Versions are compared using the right rules
div.p: Debian, RPM, Alpine, npm, Python, Maven and Go each order versions differently, and comparing them as text gets the answer wrong. Where a comparison cannot be made properly the finding is marked informational or low rather than asserted.

div.b: The finding is tracked over time
div.p: A finding that stops appearing is not automatically a fixed one. If the package is still installed at a newer version it is mitigated; if it is gone it is removed; if the host simply stopped reporting it is unknown. Silence is never counted as success.

panel.title: How MITRE ATT&CK fits, and where it loses information

div.div:
a specific vulnerability
in a specific product

the class of mistake
e.g. use-after-free

a pattern of attack
that abuses it

what an adversary
could then do

div.p: Every hop is a mapping MITRE publishes, and every hop loses information. A CVE with no CWE recorded simply never reaches the matrix, so a technique missing from the ATT&CK page is not a technique you are safe from. And because one weakness maps to several techniques, a single vulnerability is drawn several times — the widths never add up to a total.

What this chain says is “this class of weakness is the kind of thing that enables that technique”. It does not say an adversary used it, and it does not say this vulnerability is exploitable in your environment. For that, use the KEV and EPSS columns on Findings, which are about real-world exploitation rather than classification.

panel.title: How much survives the chain, right now

search.query: | `riskability_open_findings` | stats dc(cve_id) AS n | eval stage = "1. open CVEs" | append [| `riskability_finding_cwes` | stats dc(cve_id) AS n | eval stage = "2. have a CWE recorded"] | append [| `riskability_attack_surface` | stats dc(cve_id) AS n | eval stage = "3. reach a technique"] | eval series = stage | fields stage, series, n

viz.option: No open findings to trace through the chain.

html.div: The drop between these bars is not a defect — it is what the mapping costs. Read the ATT&CK page as “capabilities our open findings could hand an attacker”, never as a complete picture of exposure.

div.span: The numbers, and how stale they are.
What to patch, ranked by likelihood of exploitation rather than by severity score. This is the working list.
What actually got fixed, with the version change that proves it — and what merely stopped being reported.
Lossy classification of what your open findings could enable. Context, not evidence.
One machine at a time, split by the filesystem root each component came from.
What the app cannot see: ecosystems present in the fleet that the imported feed knows nothing about. The most honest page here.
Findings someone has decided to handle another way, with what that way is. Excluded from every risk number, and counted separately so they are never hidden.
Import the offline CVE data, and download the builder that makes it.

dl.dd: One specific vulnerability in one specific product, with an identifier everyone shares.
The class of programming mistake behind it. Most CVEs never get one assigned.
A catalogued pattern of attack that abuses such a weakness.
MITRE's catalogue of what adversaries actually do, organised by tactic. Reached here through CWE and CAPEC, so lossily.
A package URL — an identity read from a package manager's own records. Precise.
A vendor/product naming scheme used when no package manager was involved. Inferred, so weaker evidence.
A published estimate of how likely a CVE is to be exploited in the next 30 days. Better for prioritising than a severity score.
CISA's list of vulnerabilities known to be exploited in the wild right now. The strongest signal available offline.
Which filesystem the component was found in: the host itself, a snap base, a container image, a chroot.
How strong the evidence is, not how bad the vulnerability is. high means both identity and version came from package records.
Who said this version is affected — the distribution, the upstream ecosystem, or NVD. Distributions win, because they backport.
One complete import of the feed. Findings are always matched against a single generation, never a half-written one.
